name: Plumbago Grey
lede: Plumbago Grey is a pale, purplish grey named for plumbago, a word that means both a blue-flowered garden shrub and the old name for graphite, though this swatch favors neither plant blue nor pencil black.

sections.title: Two plumbagos, one grey
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 color standards place this hue on plate L, hue 61'''', tone d; it is reproduced from a scan of an aged plate, so the printed color is approximate [1]. The ISCC-NBS system later filed it in block 227, "purplish gray", and Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary also records it, on plate 44 B 4 [2][3]. "Plumbago" names both the shrub Plumbago auriculata, grown for its clear sky-blue flowers, and, in Latin, lead ore, the old word for graphite before "carbon" took over [1]. This swatch is far greyer and paler than either the flower's blue or graphite's near-black [1].

The nearest named colors in our data are [[irisglow|Irisglow]], 3.0 CIEDE2000 units away, and [[platinum-grey|Platinum Grey]] and [[manatee|Manatee]] close behind [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Plumbago Grey appears in 277 of our 23,781 paintings, about 1.16 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 146, more common than 65 percent of our named colors [4]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 23 of 1,674 paintings, at 1.6 times the expected rate for that century, and is most over-represented in Swiss paintings, at 4.3 times expected, and in Impressionist works, at 4.3 times expected [4]. Inside a painting it most often sits as a light, in 45 percent of the 146 paintings where it carries real area [4].

Its most devoted painter is Rosa Bonheur, at 5.9 times the baseline of the museums her work comes from, in 4 of her 24 works here [4]. The earliest match is dated 1119, 793 years before Ridgway's 1912 record of the name, as photographed, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [4].
